young.html: William James was a Harvard professor and one of the first people to study the mind as a science. He wanted to know: how do we pay attention? How do habits form? What is a feeling?
James noticed that your thoughts never stop. They flow from one thing to the next, like a river. He called this the stream of consciousness.

He also noticed that the more you do something, the easier it gets, like a path through grass that gets clearer each time you walk it. That is a habit. Good habits, he said, are worth building early, because they make life easier for years.

young.name: gb-james-habit
young.cap: Move the slider: each repetition wears the path deeper and the task takes less effort. (A picture of the idea, not real measurements.)

young.html: A habit experiment. Choose one small good habit, like putting your shoes in the same place or reading five minutes before bed. Do it every day for two weeks and mark a calendar. James had a rule: do not skip, especially at first. Was it easier by the end?

full.html: William James (1842–1910), elder brother of the novelist Henry James, studied painting and then medicine, and in 1872 began teaching anatomy and physiology at Harvard. He set up one of the first teaching laboratories for psychology in the 1870s, and in 1878 agreed to write a textbook. It took twelve years. The Principles of Psychology (1890), in two volumes and about 1,400 pages, mixed physiology, laboratory findings, careful self-observation and lively writing. A shorter version followed in 1892. James later turned to philosophy and religion, becoming a founder of pragmatism and writing The Varieties of Religious Experience (1902).

James begins with the brain and the nervous system, and soon comes to habit. Living matter, he says, is plastic: it can be shaped, and once shaped it keeps the form, like a fold in paper. So repeated actions become easier, more exact, and need less attention.

full.text: The great thing, then, in all education, is to make our nervous system our ally instead of our enemy.
full.author: William James
full.work: The Principles of Psychology, Chapter IV (Habit)
full.ed: Henry Holt and Company, New York

full.html: He gives practical rules (our summary): start a new habit with as strong a beginning as possible; never allow an exception until it is firmly rooted; act on every good resolution at the first chance; and keep the power of effort alive with a little unneeded effort each day.

full.name: gb-james-habit
full.cap: An illustration of James's picture of habit.

full.text: Consciousness, then, does not appear to itself chopped up in bits. Such words as 'chain' or 'train' do not describe it fitly as it presents itself in the first instance. It is nothing jointed; it flows. A 'river' or a 'stream' are the metaphors by which it is most naturally described.
full.author: William James
full.work: The Principles of Psychology, Chapter IX (The Stream of Thought)
full.ed: Henry Holt and Company, New York

full.html: Thought, James says, is always personal, always changing, continuous, and always about something, and it is always choosing, attending to some things and ignoring others. Novelists such as Virginia Woolf and James Joyce later took up "stream of consciousness" as a way of writing.

full.text: Every one knows what attention is. It is the taking possession by the mind, in clear and vivid form, of one out of what seem several simultaneously possible objects or trains of thought. Focalization, concentration, of consciousness are of its essence.
full.author: William James
full.work: The Principles of Psychology, Chapter XI (Attention)
full.ed: Henry Holt and Company, New York

full.html: James's most surprising idea turns common sense around. We usually think we see a bear, feel afraid, and then run. James argued that the body reacts first, and the emotion is our feeling of those bodily changes. The Danish physician Carl Lange reached a similar idea at about the same time, so it is called the James-Lange theory.

full.name: gb-james-emotion
full.cap: Switch between common sense and James's order.

full.html: Much of James has lasted. Research on skills and the brain supports his picture of habit becoming automatic with practice; his account of attention as limited and selective set the questions for a century of experiments. His theory of emotion was challenged by the physiologist Walter Cannon in 1927, who argued that bodily changes are too slow and too similar to tell emotions apart; later studies found that the body's state does shape feeling, but that how we interpret a situation matters too, so most psychologists today hold mixed views. Some of the Principles, such as its physiology, is simply out of date. In his shorter textbook of 1892 James called psychology "only the hope of a science," a modest view that helped keep the field open to evidence.
Thinking James was only a laboratory scientist. He trusted careful self-observation as much as experiments, and he wrote as much about free will, the self and religious experience as about nerves.

items: Aristotle's On the Soul and Locke's Essay, earlier on this ladder, also asked how experience builds the mind; James replaced Locke's separate "ideas" with a flowing stream.
Darwin taught James to see the mind as an evolved tool for survival, and habits and instincts as part of our animal inheritance.
Freud, the next great psychologist on this ladder, explored the parts of the mind outside awareness that James also wrote about.
The Memory Ladder's topics on attention and long-term memory take up questions James raised.
Do you control your habits, or do your habits control you?
Can you notice your own stream of thoughts without changing it?
Do you smile because you are happy, or can smiling make you happier?
Why is paying attention a kind of choice?

questions: What is a good habit someone in your family has? How did they build it?
Try to notice your thoughts for one minute. Where did they wander?
When you are scared, what happens in your body first?
What makes it hard to pay attention? What helps?
James said to act on a good resolution right away. Why might waiting make it harder?
